title: Can computers think? — Chinese Room argument

sources.citation: A. M. Turing. Computing Machinery and Intelligence. Mind 59 (1950).
John R. Searle. Minds, Brains, and Programs. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3 (1980).

claims.title: Machines can think
claims.statement: Machines can think. A digital computer, suitably organized, is not merely a model of a mind. It is a candidate for thought.
claims.normalizationNote: Focus claim normalized as the large answer to the issue question.

claims.title: The imitation game
claims.statement: If a machine plays the imitation game so well that an interrogator cannot reliably tell it from a human, we ought to say that it thinks.

claims.title: Thought is not bound to a biological substrate
claims.statement: Thought is not bound to a biological substrate. What matters is the organization of a discrete-state process, not the flesh that happens to realize it.

claims.title: A digital computer is a universal discrete-state machine
claims.statement: A digital computer is a universal discrete-state machine. In principle it can mimic any other discrete-state process, including whatever process we take thinking to be.

claims.title: Behavioral indistinguishability warrants ascribing thought
claims.statement: Behavioral indistinguishability is sufficient warrant for ascribing thought. We have no better test for other human minds; we should not demand a stricter one of machines.

claims.title: The Chinese Room can produce intelligible answers without understanding Chinese
claims.statement: A man locked in a room, following a rule book to shuffle Chinese symbols, can produce answers Chinese speakers find intelligible without understanding a word of Chinese.

claims.title: The man in the room implements the program
claims.statement: The man in the room is doing exactly what a computer does: manipulating formal symbols according to rules specified purely by their shape.

claims.title: Syntax is not sufficient for semantics
claims.statement: A computer program is purely formal and syntactic. Syntax is not sufficient for semantics. Formal symbol manipulation is not, by itself, a sufficient condition for thinking.

claims.title: A simulation of thought does not itself think
claims.statement: The computer, like the man in the room, does not understand. It at most simulates thinking. A simulation of digestion does not digest; a simulation of thought does not think.

claims.title: The whole system can understand even if the man does not
claims.statement: The man does not understand Chinese. The system of which he is a part — man, rule book, paper, and symbols — does. Understanding is a property of the whole.

claims.title: Internalizing the system still does not produce understanding
claims.statement: Suppose the man memorizes the rules and symbols and performs the manipulations in his head. He is now the system. He still does not understand Chinese.

subarguments.title: Is formal symbol manipulation sufficient for understanding?
subarguments.issueQuestion: Is formal symbol manipulation sufficient for understanding?

extensions.x-method: Normalized using the staged argumentation-mapping method documented in Robert E. Horn's Introduction to Argumentation Mapping (2003).
